BBG's Simon White: nominal yields have in the main risen this year not because fiscal risks are expected to get even worse (or, equivalently, because inflation is about to become unanchored) - but because real growth is expected to rise

The economy's resilience can be seen in the chart below, showing that now none of the Fed's six regional manufacturing indices are in contraction. When all are rising, that has historically often coincided with a recession. That none are, shows that an imminent recession (say in 3-6 months) has quite a low probability.

The flipside of all this is that a magic level in yields is unlikely to trigger a durable and significant rally. Instead, we're not likely to see such a move until real growth or inflation are slowing.

🚨 🇺🇲 Next week, Nvidia could absolutely crush earnings expectations on Tuesday and still see its stock collapse.

📊 Wall Street expects around $109 billion in third-quarter revenue representing 90% YoY growth followed by almost $125 billion in the fourth quarter. Absolutely insane numbers but how much longer its customers can afford to keep buying its GPUs ? Nvidia has become much more than a chip supplier as it's now actively financing parts of its own ecosystem through investments, financial guarantees, and massive supply commitments. Its latest financial filings revealed approximately $530 billion in commitments and exposures of various kinds, including $279 billion in supply and capacity commitments. Nvidia helps finance companies building data centers that ultimately purchase Nvidia's own GPUs. As long as capital keeps flowing, the machine works, but if these infrastructure investments fail to generate sufficient returns, the entire system becomes much more vulnerable.

➡️ Jensen Huang's departure changes many things. We're talking about a CEO who personally controlled an extraordinary number of Nvidia's strategic, commercial, and financial decisions. Colette Kress, now serving as interim CEO, had reportedly already pushed back against some of Huang's more aggressive financing initiatives. If she decides to scale back the guarantees and investments Nvidia provides to its partners, from a growth perspective, it could create serious problems. Less financing potentially means fewer data centers getting built, which means GPU orders being pushed further into the future, and all of this is happening while financing conditions are tightening, major technology companies are borrowing heavily, and the Democrats' takeover of Congress could introduce additional obstacles for certain infrastructure projects.

⚠️ The stock has already corrected significantly and the company continues to generate extraordinary amounts of cash. A strong quarter combined with reassuring guidance could easily trigger a violent relief rally. However, if Nvidia delivers exceptional results but starts talking about delayed projects, reduced visibility into 2027–2028, or a reassessment of its financial commitments, I would take that extremely seriously. 

Next Tuesday will especially be about how long the company can sustain this kind of growth without having to help finance the demand for its own products.

If Jensen returns, it would not be without precedent…

Sam Altman was abruptly fired as CEO of OpenAI on Friday, November 17, 2023, only to be reinstated five days later on November 21, 2023, following a massive revolt by employees and major investors
---
FYI

On Nov 17, 2023, OpenAI’s nonprofit board abruptly fired CEO Sam Altman. Just five days later (Nov 21), he was reinstated after Microsoft offered to hire him and >95% of OpenAI’s staff threatened to quit unless the board stepped down.

* A total breakdown in trust between Altman and the board (not fraud or a specific AI safety failure). Key friction points included:

* Lack of candor: Board members felt kept in the dark on major moves (e.g., finding out about ChatGPT’s launch on Twitter and Altman’s ownership of the OpenAI Startup Fund externally).

* Internal friction: Senior leaders accused Altman of pitting executives against each other, and board members felt he tried to manipulate them into ousting director Helen Toner over a critical research paper.

* Governance clash: A small, safety-focused nonprofit board held absolute firing power over a CEO aggressively scaling a hyper-growth commercial business.
--
If Elon or someone else hires Jensen, is the board afraid he’ll take hundreds of its best employees with him?

China confirmed fresh U.S.–China tariff discussions ahead of Thursday’s expected Trump–Xi meeting. No agreement announced yet. For industrial metals, actual tariff relief could matter far more than diplomatic headlines.

My takeaway: nuclear ambitions are increasingly translating into funded fuel commitments.

🥈 SILVER — THE DEFICIT NEEDS CONTEXT

The Silver Institute’s latest outlook forecasts a sixth consecutive annual deficit: 35 million ounces in 2026. But total demand is expected to fall 5%, with solar thrifting and substitution weighing on consumption.

Industrial demand outside solar is forecast to grow 4.5%. A mixed picture, and a reminder that deficits alone don’t guarantee rising prices.

🥇 GOLD — INFLATION ISN’T AUTOMATICALLY BULLISH

Friday’s U.S. PPI rose 0.3% monthly and 6.5% annually. Gold’s difficult week showed how expectations of higher interest rates can overwhelm inflation-hedge demand. I’m watching whether yields and the dollar ease enough to give bullion breathing room.

AI investment worries weighed on copper, yet Shanghai exchange inventories fell another 18.3% last week and import premiums hit a record.

That divergence deserves attention: falling prices alongside shrinking available stocks.

159 years ago today, the first stock ticker tape debuted… 

On November 15, 1867, the first stock ticker debuted in New York City, changing how quickly investors could follow the market. 

Developed by Edward Calahan, the machine transmitted stock quotes over telegraph wires and printed them on paper tape, earning its name from the ticking sound it made. 

Investors who had relied on messengers to deliver prices could now receive updates directly, making it easier to track trading beyond the exchange floor. 

It’s easy to take instant quotes for granted today, but 159 years ago, a strip of paper represented a major technological advance on Wall Street.

The more I hang out with top AI researchers, the more I realize how many of them are exploring architectures beyond the standard Transformer.

JEPA, diffusion models, Mamba, state-space models, etc. So many radically different approaches being explored in parallel.

It seems almost inconceivable that we won’t see a major architectural breakthrough.

And by breakthrough, I mean something that delivers better frontier intelligence with significantly less training compute.

That doesn’t mean we’ll use less compute overall. Quite the opposite, total compute consumption will keep growing. But we’ll get much better performance for every unit of compute spent.
